title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: M1's verbless sentence doing its most useful work: al-kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila is a whole sentence — "the book is on the table" — with no "is" anywhere in it. Every location sentence in this module is built that way.

The place words stay separate words and never fuse with the article: fī al-bayt, ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila, taḥt al-kitāb, amām al-madrasa. Written in full even though speech runs them together (fi l-bayt) — the elision belongs in the sound line, never in the spelling.

fī arrives as a word of its own. Until now it only came welded into time phrases — fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ, fī al-layl, fī al-bayt — and it is the same preposition all along: "in, at". From here it can go in front of any place at all.

hunāka and the plain sentence say two different things, and it is al- that carries the difference: hunāka kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila asserts that a book EXISTS there, and its noun is indefinite; al-kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila says where a known book is. English has one "there is / it is" for both.

The iḍāfa: two nouns pushed together to say one belongs to the other. In bāb al-bayt ("the door of the house") the POSSESSED noun comes first and takes NO al- even though it is definite, and only the last noun carries the article. *al-bāb al-bayt is wrong — the one place M1's "a general noun keeps al-" is overruled.

"iḍāfa is just of" is the slogan to refuse. It is not English word order with "of" deleted; it is a rule about which noun may wear the article, and the order decides the meaning: bāb al-bayt is the house's door, bayt al-bāb would be the door's house.

The other way to possess is M1's suffix, unchanged: bayt + -ī = baytī (my house), baytuka (your-m), baytuki (your-f), baytuhu (his). A noun ending in the silent -a of sayyāra brings a real t back under the suffix: sayyāra becomes sayyāratī.

ʿind- is how Arabic HAS things, and there is no verb in it: ʿindī sayyāra is literally "at-me a car". It is a preposition with a person suffix — ʿindī, ʿindaka, ʿindaki, ʿindahu — so the sentence stays verbless like every other one here.

English "to have" is a plain verb, so a learner goes looking for one; there is none to find. And because ʿind- makes a verbless sentence, negating it would need laysa, which L1 never teaches — so every ʿind- sentence in this level is affirmative.
ayna asks where and stands at the front, and the answer comes back as the same verbless sentence: ayna al-kitāb? — al-kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila. Nothing is added and nothing moves.

Sun letters keep earning their keep across this module's nouns: aṭ-ṭāwila and as-sayyāra assimilate, al-kitāb and al-bayt do not. Each spelling is its own key in the word index, so write them the way M2 decided.

sentences.cue: The book is on the table

words.note: kitāb is a book — the writing-thing, from the same root as "write". k is a moon letter, so al- keeps its l: al-kitāb. Bare kitāb is "a book", and M8 will count them.
"On", resting on top of something. It opens with ʿayn, not hamza — ʿalā is a different letter from the ʾ of māʾ, and this course keeps the two apart. A separate word, never joined to what follows.
ṭāwila is a table. ṭ is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and is written as it is said: aṭ-ṭāwila, never *al-ṭāwila — the same spelling law as ash-shāy and aṣ-ṣabāḥ.

sentences.trap: There is no "is" to look for and nothing missing: noun, preposition, noun, and the sentence is finished.
sentences.sound: al-ki-TAAB ʿa-LAA aṭ-ṬAA-wi-la — the ṭ is heavy and pulls the vowel after it down with it.

variations.cue: The key is on the table
variations.changed: swap what is on the table — the frame holds

variations.cue: A book is on the table
variations.changed: drop al- and the book stops being a known one

mistake.why: English needs its "is", so huwa ("he, it") gets pressed into service. The present affirmative has no copula at all — M1's first law, still running: al-kitāb ʿalā aṭ-ṭāwila.

sentences.usage: Answering "where is it?" — the flattest, most useful sentence in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: kitāb — the thing that is written; maktaba, the library, is the place full of them.

sentences.cue: The key is under the book

words.note: "Under", the opposite of ʿalā. The ḥ in the middle is the breathy one — a hard whisper from the throat, not the h of hal.
miftāḥ is a key — the opening-tool, built the way maṭʿam was built from food and madrasa from studying. m is a moon letter, so al- keeps its l.

sentences.trap: taḥt and ʿalā take the noun straight, with no extra word between them: taḥt al-kitāb, not *taḥt min al-kitāb.
sentences.sound: al-mif-TAAḤ TAḤT al-ki-TAAB — both words end on the same breathy ḥ.

variations.cue: The key is under the table
variations.changed: book → table: the preposition does not care what follows it

variations.cue: The book is under the key
variations.changed: swap the two nouns and the sentence swaps with them

mistake.why: Meant as "under the book", this says "under a book" — any book. The article is what points at the one on the table: taḥt al-kitāb.

sentences.usage: Where something has gone — the sentence you say while looking for it.
sentences.mnemonic: miftāḥ — what opens (fataḥa, to open); taḥt is what is beneath.

words.note: "Where", standing at the front like M4's matā ("when") and M2's kayfa ("how"). It needs no hal beside it — a question word is already the question.

sentences.trap: No hal here. hal is for yes/no questions; ayna, matā and kayfa ask for an answer and do the job themselves.
sentences.sound: AY-na al-ki-TAAB — ayna rhymes with "liner" cut short.

variations.cue: Where is the table?
variations.changed: ask after anything: ayna takes any noun

variations.cue: Where are you? (to a man)
variations.changed: a person instead of a thing — still no verb

mistake.why: Two question markers on one question. hal turns a statement into a yes/no question; ayna already asks. One or the other: ayna al-kitāb?

sentences.usage: The question this whole module answers.

sentences.cue: There is a book on the table

words.note: hunāka does two jobs with one word: it points somewhere ("over there") and it announces that something exists ("there is"). In the second job the noun after it is INDEFINITE — hunāka kitāb, a book, not the book.

sentences.trap: English "there is a book" and "the book is there" look like one sentence; Arabic splits them by the article. hunāka kitāb introduces; al-kitāb hunāka locates.

variations.cue: The book is on the table
variations.changed: drop hunāka and add al-: a known book, located

variations.cue: There is a school in front of the house
variations.changed: the same announcement about a different thing

mistake.why: Meant as "there is a book", but with al- the only reading left is the pointing one — "over there, the book is on the table". Announcing that something exists takes the bare noun: hunāka kitāb.

sentences.usage: Telling someone what is in a room they cannot see.
sentences.mnemonic: hunāka — "hun-there": the word points and announces at once.

sentences.cue: The car is in front of the house

words.note: "In front of" — one Arabic word for what English needs three of. Like taḥt and ʿalā it takes its noun straight, with nothing in between: amām al-bayt.

sentences.trap: One word, not three. amām al-bayt is complete; there is no "of" to add and no "the front" to name.
sentences.sound: as-say-YAA-ra a-MAAM al-BAYT — sayyāra holds its doubled y.

variations.cue: The car is in front of the school
variations.changed: swap the landmark

variations.cue: There is a car in front of the house
variations.changed: hunāka and a bare noun: announcing instead of locating

mistake.why: s is a sun letter, so the article assimilates: as-sayyāra. al-sayyāra is not another spelling of the word — in this course it is no word at all, exactly as with al-shāy in M2.

sentences.usage: Telling someone where you parked, or which building is which.
sentences.mnemonic: amām — what is "ahead of" you; the a-m-m of "in front".

sentences.cue: Rohan is at the market today

words.note: The fī you already know from fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ and fī al-bayt, now standing on its own in front of any place: fī as-sūq, fī al-maṭʿam, fī al-madrasa. Written in full even though it is said fi l-, running into the article behind it.

sentences.trap: fī does not shorten on the page. It is pronounced fi l-sūq and written fī as-sūq — one word, one spelling, whatever speech does to it.
sentences.sound: ro-HAAN fi s-SOOQ al-YAWM — the fī melts into the article and the s doubles.

variations.cue: Rohan is at the restaurant
variations.changed: any place at all follows fī

variations.cue: I am at home today
variations.changed: a person instead of a name — and the sentence still has no verb

mistake.why: The verb M6 taught in the future gets pressed into the present. yakūn is for what generally is or what will be, never for where somebody is standing right now — that sentence has no verb in it at all: Rohān fī as-sūq al-yawm.

sentences.usage: Saying where somebody is right now.
sentences.mnemonic: fī — "fee": in, at, inside; the shortest word in the module.

sentences.cue: The door of the house is big

words.note: bāb is a door — and here it is the first half of an iḍāfa, so it wears NO article even though "the door of the house" is perfectly definite. The article sits on the last noun only: bāb al-bayt. Its own definiteness is borrowed from what follows it.

sentences.trap: The first noun of an iḍāfa may never take al-. *al-bāb al-bayt is the English shape ("the door of the house") pushed word for word into Arabic, and it breaks the construction.
sentences.sound: BAAB al-BAYT ka-BEER — three heavy syllables, no joining words at all.

variations.cue: The door of the school is big
variations.changed: swap the second noun — the first keeps its bare shape

variations.cue: The car door is big
variations.changed: English drops "of" here too; Arabic writes exactly the same two nouns

mistake.why: Two articles kill the iḍāfa. Only the LAST noun carries al-, and the first is definite because of it: bāb al-bayt. With al- on both, the two nouns stop belonging to each other.

sentences.usage: Describing a building, a car, a room — anything made of parts that belong to it.
sentences.mnemonic: bāb al-bayt — door-of-house, in that order, and only the house gets a the.

words.note: There is no verb "to have" in Arabic. ʿind- means "at, by", and the person is the same suffix as M1's ismī: ʿindī (at me = I have), ʿindaka (you-m), ʿindaki (you-f), ʿindahu (he). The sentence stays verbless, so what you have comes after it bare: ʿindī sayyāra.

sentences.trap: Do not look for a verb. "I have a car" is two words in Arabic and neither of them is one — and the thing owned is the subject, sitting there without an article.
sentences.sound: ʿIN-dee say-YAA-ra ka-BEE-ra — the ʿ opens the word from deep in the throat.

variations.cue: You have a big car (to a man)
variations.changed: -ī → -aka: the same possession, moved to you

variations.cue: He has a book
variations.changed: -ahu: his, and a different thing owned

mistake.why: English needs its "I", so anā sneaks in. The -ī of ʿindī already says me — anā on top reads as emphasis, not as plain speech. The same law as M1's uḥibb and M5's dhahabtu.

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone says about what they own.
sentences.mnemonic: ʿindī — "in-dee", at me: what is at you is what you have.

sentences.cue: My car is in front of the school

words.note: M3's sayyāra with M1's -ī welded on. The silent -a at the end of sayyāra is a hidden t, and a suffix wakes it up: sayyāra becomes sayyārat-ī, sayyārat-uka, sayyārat-uki. Every noun ending that way does the same.

sentences.trap: The t is not added, it was always there. sayyāra ends in a letter that is silent alone and pronounced under a suffix — so sayyāratī is one word, not two.
sentences.sound: say-yaa-ra-TEE a-MAAM al-MAD-ra-sa — the ending pulls the stress onto itself.

variations.cue: Your car is in front of the school (to a man)
variations.changed: -ī → -uka: whose car it is

variations.cue: The car is in front of the school
variations.changed: the article instead of the suffix — a car, not my car

mistake.why: The hidden t left out — and the Arabic shows it too, with the closed ة still sitting where an open ت belongs. Under a suffix that ending becomes a real t: sayyāratī, سيارتي.

sentences.usage: Pointing out what is yours in a street full of things that are not.
sentences.mnemonic: sayyārat-ī — the t wakes up when someone owns it.

sentences.cue: My house is near the market

words.note: M3's bayt with the possessive suffix: baytī (my), baytuka (your-m), baytuki (your-f), baytuhu (his). A noun wearing a suffix never also wears al- — baytī is already "my house", so *al-baytī is impossible.

"Near" — qarīb of a masculine thing, qarība of a feminine one. It takes min after it, not "to": qarīb min as-sūq, near FROM the market. M6's qarīban ("soon") is this same word wearing the adverbial ending.

sentences.trap: Near takes min, where English takes "to". qarīb min as-sūq is the fixed pair — M1's min ("from") doing a second job.
sentences.sound: bay-TEE qa-REEB min as-SOOQ — both q's come from the very back of the throat.

variations.cue: My house is near the school
variations.changed: swap the landmark

variations.cue: My car is near the house
variations.changed: a feminine subject, so the adjective takes -a

mistake.why: The article and the possessive suffix cannot both be on one noun. The suffix already makes it definite: baytī, my house. al-bayt is the house; baytī is my house; there is no third thing.

sentences.usage: Explaining where you live by what it is next to.
sentences.mnemonic: baytī — my bayt; add the -ī and drop the al-, always.

comprehensionPool.cue: The key is on the table
Where is your car? (to a man)
There is a school in front of the house
The book is under the table
You have a big car (to a man)
The door of the school is big
My house is near the school
